details:
**Allegory of the Cave**
The most famous passage of the Republic, at the start of Book VII. Prisoners chained in a cave see only shadows cast on a wall by objects carried in front of a fire, and they take those shadows for reality. One prisoner is freed and makes a hard climb out into the sunlight. The story illustrates Plato's Theory of Forms and the role of philosophical education. It is the most common giveaway.

**Philosopher-kings**
Plato's ideal rulers. Socrates argues that cities will have no rest from trouble until philosophers rule or rulers become philosophers, because only philosophers know the Form of the Good. The work lays out a long education for them, including mathematics and geometry.

**Ring of Gyges**
A story Glaucon tells in Book II. A Lydian shepherd finds a ring that makes him invisible, then uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king, and take the throne. Glaucon uses the story to argue that people are just only out of fear of being caught, and he challenges Socrates to show that justice is worth having for its own sake.

**Noble Lie (Myth of Metals)**
A founding myth proposed in Book III. Citizens are told they were born from the earth and that the god mixed gold, silver, or bronze and iron into their souls, which fixes their places as rulers, auxiliaries, or farmers and craftsmen. Belief in the myth is meant to keep the classes content and the city stable.

**The Divided Line**
An analogy in Book VI that divides a line into the visible realm and the intelligible realm, and then subdivides each. The four segments run from images and shadows (illusion), to physical objects (belief), to mathematical reasoning, to understanding of the Forms (the highest, philosophical knowledge).

**Analogy of the Sun and the Form of the Good**
In Book VI, Socrates compares the Form of the Good to the sun. Just as the sun gives light that lets us see and also makes things grow, the Good makes the Forms knowable and is the source of their being.

**Myth of Er**
The story that ends the Republic in Book X. Er, a soldier who seems to have died in battle, revives on his funeral pyre and describes the afterlife. He sees the just rewarded and the unjust punished, the Spindle of Necessity that turns the heavenly bodies, and souls choosing their next lives by lottery.

**Thrasymachus: "Justice is the advantage of the stronger"**
In Book I, the sophist Thrasymachus argues that justice is simply whatever benefits those in power. Socrates spends much of the dialogue answering this challenge, along with Glaucon's.

**Cephalus, Polemarchus, and the opening definitions of justice**
The dialogue opens at the house of the old man Cephalus in the Piraeus, after his son Polemarchus urges Socrates to stay. Cephalus suggests justice is telling the truth and paying what you owe. Socrates refutes this with the case of returning weapons to a friend who has gone mad, and Polemarchus then defines justice as helping friends and harming enemies.

**Ship of State**
An analogy in Book VI. A strong but deaf and shortsighted shipowner is surrounded by quarreling sailors who seize the ship, while they dismiss the true navigator as a useless "stargazer." It shows how democracies ignore those with real knowledge.

**Guardians, auxiliaries, and producers (the tripartite city and soul)**
The ideal city, sometimes called Kallipolis, has three classes: guardian rulers, auxiliaries (soldiers), and producers. They match the three parts of the soul: reason, spirit, and appetite. Justice means each part does its own job without interfering with the others. Guardians give up private property and share wives and children in common.

**Banishing the poets (the three beds)**
In Book X, Socrates argues that poets and painters are imitators who know nothing of the truth. There are three beds: the Form of the bed made by god, the bed made by a carpenter, and a painting of a bed, which is an imitation of an imitation. Most poetry is therefore banished from the ideal city.

**Decline of regimes**
In Books VIII and IX, Socrates describes how the ideal aristocracy decays, starting when rulers fail to breed the right successors. It declines through timocracy, oligarchy, and democracy into tyranny. The tyrant is called the most miserable man because he is a slave to his own passions.

**Karl Popper's The Open Society and Its Enemies**
Popper's first volume, "The Spell of Plato," attacks the Republic as a blueprint for a totalitarian state. He criticizes its noble lie, its censorship of art, and its raising of children apart from their parents.

**The painted statue (purple eyes)**
An analogy in Book IV. One would not paint a statue's eyes purple, the most beautiful color, if that ruined the whole statue. In the same way, the city should make the whole community happy rather than giving any one class, even the guardians, the greatest happiness.
